f-w-de-klerk: Frederik Willem de Klerk was born on 18 March 1936 in Mayfair, a suburb of Johannesburg, into an influential Afrikaner family with long ties to the National Party. His father Jan de Klerk was a senator, president of the senate for seven years, acting state president and a cabinet member for fifteen years. His aunt's husband, J. G. Strijdom, was a former prime minister, and his brother Willem later left the party to found the liberal Democratic Party. De Klerk studied at Potchefstroom University from 1954 to 1958, took degrees in arts and law, and was initiated into the Broederbond. He set up a law partnership in Vereeniging in 1962. In 1972 he was elected to the House of Assembly.

As a minister in the government of P. W. Botha, de Klerk supported and enforced apartheid. After Botha resigned as party leader, de Klerk defeated Barend du Plessis, 69 votes to 61, and was elected leader of the National Party on 2 February 1989. Botha resigned the presidency on 14 August 1989, and de Klerk was elected State President on 20 September. ANC leaders and Desmond Tutu doubted that he would differ from his predecessors, but he allowed a protest march of about 30,000 people in Cape Town to proceed, saying the door to a new South Africa was open.

His presidency was dominated by negotiations between his government and the ANC. In a whites-only referendum on 17 March 1992 more than two thirds voted to continue negotiating an end to apartheid. State security forces committed widespread human rights abuses and encouraged violence between Xhosa and Zulu people, though de Klerk later denied sanctioning such actions. Mandela distrusted de Klerk's role, particularly regarding the so-called third force, and the question was never clarified. In 1993 de Klerk publicly apologised for apartheid's harmful effects. After the 1994 election he served as one of two deputy presidents, and he opposed the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, preferring a blanket amnesty. In May 1996 the National Party withdrew from the coalition.

De Klerk retired from active politics in 1997 and lectured internationally. His autobiography The Last Trek appeared in 1999. He died on 11 November 2021 at his home in Cape Town, a few months after a diagnosis of mesothelioma. Afterwards the F. W. de Klerk Foundation released a video in which he apologised without qualification for the harm caused by apartheid. He was a controversial figure. Anti-apartheid activists criticised him for offering only a qualified apology and for ignoring abuses by the security forces, while supporters of apartheid held that he had betrayed the Afrikaner minority. He himself said that his views had changed completely, as in a conversion.
faisal-i-of-iraq: Faisal was born in Mecca on 20 May 1885, the third son of Hussein bin Ali, the Grand Sharif of Mecca, and grew up in Constantinople. In 1913 he was elected to the Ottoman parliament as representative of Jeddah. When the Ottoman Empire entered the war in December 1914, his father sent him to Constantinople, and on the way he met members of the Arab secret societies al-Fatat and Al-'Ahd. He joined al-Fatat. On 23 October 1916 he met Captain T. E. Lawrence, and from 1916 to 1918 he headed the Northern Army of the Great Arab Revolt against the Ottomans, with British assistance.

British and Arab forces took Damascus in October 1918, and Faisal helped set up an Arab government there. In 1919 he led the Arab delegation to the Paris Peace Conference, and on 4 January 1919 he signed an agreement with the Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann, which he accepted only conditionally. On 8 March 1920 the Syrian National Congress proclaimed him king of the Arab Kingdom of Syria. After the San Remo conference gave France the Mandate for Syria and Lebanon, the French defeated his forces at the Battle of Maysalun on 24 July 1920 and expelled him from Syria.

At the Cairo Conference in March 1921 the British chose Faisal to rule their Mandate of Iraq, partly on the advice of Lawrence. A plebiscite reported 96 per cent in favour, and he was made king on 23 August 1921, though few Iraqis knew him and the Shia majority was at first lukewarm. He encouraged pan-Arab nationalism and sought unity between Sunni and Shia, though equating Iraqi patriotism with being Arab marginalised the Kurds. In 1932 Iraq became independent and entered the League of Nations. Faisal died of a heart attack in Bern on 8 September 1933, aged 48, and was succeeded by his eldest son Ghazi.
falklands-war: The war was a major episode in a long dispute over sovereignty. Argentina claims the islands as its own territory and described its action as the reclamation of that territory, while the British government regarded it as an invasion of a territory that had been a Crown colony since 1841. The Falkland Islanders, who have lived on the islands since the early 19th century, are mostly descendants of British settlers and strongly favoured British sovereignty. In 1965 the United Nations called on both states to settle the dispute, and talks made little progress, since the islanders refused to consider Argentine sovereignty. Argentina in 1981 was in economic stagnation and widespread unrest against the military junta that had governed since 1976.

On 2 April 1982 Argentine forces made amphibious landings, known as Operation Rosario, on the Falkland Islands. The garrison of 68 marines and 11 naval hydrographers, with 23 volunteers, offered a brief but fierce defence organised by the Governor, Sir Rex Hunt. South Georgia was invaded the next day. On 5 April the British government sent a naval task force, eventually of 127 ships, and by early May the Argentine garrison numbered around 13,000. United Nations Security Council Resolution 502 demanded the withdrawal of Argentine troops, and shuttle diplomacy by the United States Secretary of State Alexander Haig failed. Neither state formally declared war.

British forces retook South Georgia in April. On 2 May a British submarine sank the Argentine cruiser ARA General Belgrano, and on 4 May an Exocet missile struck the destroyer HMS Sheffield. British troops landed at San Carlos Water on 21 May, where Argentine air attacks gave the bay the name Bomb Alley. After the battle of Goose Green on 27 and 28 May, in which 961 Argentine personnel were taken prisoner, the British attacked the high ground round Stanley on the night of 11 June, with the hardest fighting at Mount Longdon. A ceasefire came on 14 June, when General Mario Menéndez surrendered to Major General Jeremy Moore.

In all, 649 Argentine and 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders were killed in 74 days. Patriotic feeling ran high in Argentina, but the defeat prompted large protests against the ruling military government, hastening its fall and the return of democracy. In Britain the Conservative government was re-elected with an increased majority the following year. Diplomatic relations between the two states were restored in 1989, with no change in either position on sovereignty. Britain built a permanent military complex at Mount Pleasant, opened in 1985, and the islands remain a self-governing British Overseas Territory.
fall-of-constantinople: Constantinople had been an imperial capital since 330 and had been captured only once in eleven centuries, in the Sack of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in 1204. The Nicaeans retook it in 1261 and restored the Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty. Between 1346 and 1349 the Black Death killed almost half the inhabitants. By 1453 the city was a series of walled villages separated by fields, encircled by the fifth-century Theodosian walls.

Mehmed II succeeded his father in 1451 at the age of 19, and many European courts expected little of him. In early 1452 he began building the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the European shore of the Bosphorus, which with the older Anadolu Hisarı controlled sea traffic. Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos asked Western Europe for help, but union of the eastern and western churches, agreed at the Council of Florence in 1439, met strong resistance in the city.

The Byzantines stretched a chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn and repaired the land walls. The defenders numbered under 8,000 in all. George Sphrantzes recorded 4,773 Greeks and 200 foreigners, with up to three thousand Genoese, Venetians and others who came to help, to guard a perimeter of twelve miles. The siege began on 6 April 1453. Mehmed's cannons fired on the walls for weeks, but their slow rate of fire let the Byzantines repair most of the damage after each shot.

On 28 May processions were held and the emperor attended a last Vespers in the Hagia Sophia. The final assault came on 29 May, after a siege of 53 days. The walls had protected the city for 800 years, but Ottoman infantry with the support of cannons and bombards overcame them.

Mehmed promised his soldiers three days of plunder, but later sources say he rode into the city on the first day and halted the looting. By 2 June he found the city largely deserted and half in ruins. Mehmed let Christians who had escaped capture or been ransomed return to their homes, and made Constantinople the Ottoman capital in place of Adrianople. He called himself Kayser-i Rum, Caesar of the Romans.

The fall ended the Roman Empire, which had lasted nearly 1,500 years, and many modern historians treat it as the end of the medieval period. Byzantine scholars who migrated to Italy are considered by many to have been key to the revival of Greek and Roman studies behind Renaissance humanism. The name Istanbul became official only in 1930.
fano: Fano is a coastal city of the province of Pesaro and Urbino in the Marche, twelve kilometres south-east of Pesaro, at the point where the Via Flaminia reaches the Adriatic Sea. Its ancient name, Fanum Fortunae, means Temple of Fortune, after a prominent local sanctuary dedicated to the goddess Fortuna. The remains of a monumental podium beneath the medieval convent of Saint Augustine are identified as that temple.

The settlement is first mentioned in 49 BCE, when Julius Caesar held it along with Pisaurum and Ancona. Augustus established a colony there and built a wall, parts of which remain, and in 2 CE he built an arch at the entrance to the town. In January 271 the Roman army won the Battle of Fano on the banks of the Metauro river, just inland. The Ostrogoths under Vitiges destroyed the town in 538. The Byzantines rebuilt it, and it became the capital of the maritime Pentapolis, the Five Cities, which also included Rimini, Pesaro, Senigallia and Ancona. In 754 the Frankish kings donated it to the Holy See.

The Malatesta became lords of the city in 1356 with Galeotto I Malatesta, nominally only a vicar of the popes. Pandolfo III resided in the city and was buried in the church of San Francesco in a tomb designed by Leon Battista Alberti. In 1463 papal troops under Federico III da Montefeltro besieged Roberto, son of Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, in the castle, and his peace treaty ended Malatesta rule in Fano. The siege ordered by Pope Pius II destroyed the upper storey of the Roman arch. The city was later part of the short-lived state of Cesare Borgia and then of the della Rovere duchy.

Fano had about 59,000 inhabitants in 2021. Its Arch of Augustus still stands, and the cathedral, begun in the twelfth century on the site of one burned in 1111, was restored in the 1920s. The church of Santa Maria Nuova holds two works by Perugino. A week-long festival, Fano dei Cesari, ends each summer with a parade in Roman costume and chariot races.
faroe-islands: The Faroe Islands are a group of 18 major islands, with 779 islands, islets and skerries in all, about 655 kilometres off the coast of Northern Europe, roughly halfway between Iceland and Norway. They cover 1,393 square kilometres. The islands are rugged and rocky, the coasts are mostly cliffs, and the highest point is Slættaratindur in northern Eysturoy, at 882 metres.

They consist of a succession of mostly basaltic lava about six kilometres thick, erupted in the Paleogene during the opening of the North Atlantic. The name Føroyar derives from the Old Norse Færeyjar. The most widely held theory, first attested in Færeyinga saga, reads it as sheep islands, from fær and eyjar, though others have proposed Old Irish or other origins.

Archaeological studies from 2021 found burnt grains of domesticated barley and peat ash dated between the mid-fourth and the late eighth centuries, and sheep DNA in lake sediments dating to the year 500. Because Scandinavians did not begin using sails until about 750, the study concluded that these earlier settlers more likely came from Scotland or Ireland. Færeyinga saga and Dicuil date the Norse settlement to the early 9th century, and Grímur Kamban is recorded as the first permanent settler.

The islands were first governed as an independent commonwealth under the Løgting, and they came under Norwegian rule in the early 11th century after Sigmundur Brestisson introduced Christianity. They came under de facto Danish rule after 1523. After the introduction of Lutheranism in 1538 the Faroese language was banned in public institutions and disappeared from writing for more than three centuries. The Treaty of Kiel ceded the islands to Denmark in 1814, and the Løgting was abolished in 1816 and reinstated in 1851. A referendum in 1946 produced a narrow majority for independence, which King Christian X annulled, and home rule was granted in 1948.

The Faroe Islands are an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. The capital is Tórshavn and the official language is Faroese, which is partially mutually intelligible with Icelandic. They are self-governing apart from defence, policing, justice and currency. The Løgting claims to be one of the oldest continuously running parliaments in the world.

Fishing accounts for around 90 per cent of exports. The islands did not join the European Economic Community in 1973, which left them in control of their own fishing waters. Faroese folk songs, the kvæði, were handed down orally and accompanied the medieval chain dance.
farouk-of-egypt: Farouk was born at the Abdeen Palace in Cairo on 11 February 1920, the eldest child of Sultan Fuad I, later King Fuad I, and his second wife Nazli Sabri. His family had Albanian, Circassian, Turkish, French, Greek and Egyptian ancestry. Fuad I died on 28 April 1936, and the sixteen-year-old Farouk left England to return as king, reaching Alexandria on 6 May 1936, where large crowds greeted him.

A regency council governed until 29 June 1937, when Farouk turned 17 by the Islamic lunar calendar and was counted as 18. He was crowned in Cairo on 29 July 1937. He cultivated an image as a pious king and courted the Muslim Brotherhood as a counterweight to the Wafd Party of Nahas Pasha, whose government he dismissed in the autumn of 1937. Egypt stayed neutral in the Second World War, though under British pressure he broke relations with Germany in September 1939.

Egypt ended the war as a creditor of Britain, yet wealth was very unevenly spread: the kingdom had 500 millionaires while most peasants lived in great poverty, and a cholera epidemic in 1947 killed 80,000 people. Farouk's popularity declined. British troops left the Nile valley in 1946 but kept their base on the Suez Canal. In May 1948 Farouk overruled Prime Minister Mahmoud El Nokrashy Pasha, who had warned that the army was not ready, and took Egypt into war with Israel, fearing that the Muslim Brotherhood would otherwise gain strength.

On 17 October 1951 Parliament cancelled the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936, and guerrilla attacks on the Suez base followed. On 25 January 1952 British forces besieged the police station at Ismailia, and 43 policemen and 3 soldiers were killed. The next day, 26 January 1952, known as Black Saturday, rioters burned much of downtown Cairo; 26 people died. Farouk dismissed Nahas and then changed prime ministers repeatedly over the following six months.

Farouk was overthrown in July 1952 and forced to abdicate in favour of his six-month-old son Ahmed Fuad, who reigned formally as Fuad II until the monarchy was abolished in June 1953. Farouk settled first in Naples and then in Rome. In October 1952 he was indicted for treason in Egypt, though no extradition request was made. He died in exile in Italy on 18 March 1965. His wealth and lavish way of life made him known abroad as a playboy king, and the corruption of his government was widely condemned in Egypt.
fascism: The historian Zeev Sternhell traced the ideological roots of fascism to the 1880s, to a fin de siècle revolt against materialism, rationalism, positivism, bourgeois society and democracy. The word comes from the Italian fascio, a bundle of sticks, ultimately from the Latin fasces, the bundle of rods tied round an axe that was an ancient Roman symbol of a magistrate's authority and suggested strength through unity. Fascists saw the First World War as a revolution in war, society, the state and technology.

When the war began in August 1914 the Italian left split. Benito Mussolini, expelled as chief editor of the Socialist Party's newspaper Avanti! for his anti-German stance, joined the interventionist cause, and members of his Fasces of Revolutionary Action first used the term fascism in 1915. In 1919 he founded the Italian Fasces of Combat in Milan, which became the National Fascist Party two years later.

Definition has been a long and complex debate. Historian Ian Kershaw wrote that defining fascism is like trying to nail jelly to the wall. One school, including Stanley G. Payne, Roger Griffin and Roger Eatwell, understands it as a movement based on the myth of national rebirth, and Griffin identifies palingenetic ultranationalism as its core. Scholars place it on the far right, as opposed to communism, socialism and parliamentary liberalism.

Fascism promotes a totalitarian state. Mussolini's The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), partly ghostwritten by the philosopher Giovanni Gentile, states that outside the state no human or spiritual values can exist. It treats violence as a means of national rejuvenation, and most fascist parties created their own militias, such as the Blackshirts and the Nazi Party's Sturmabteilung.

Named prime minister, Mussolini had to form a coalition government, which at first pursued economically liberal policies under the finance minister Alberto De Stefani. The Great Depression brought social unrest, and fascist propaganda blamed minorities and scapegoats. During World War II the Axis Powers in Europe, led by Nazi Germany, took part in the Holocaust, the extermination of millions of Jews, Poles, Roma, Sinti and others. In 1943 Mussolini was removed and arrested on the order of King Victor Emmanuel III, then rescued by German forces to lead the Italian Social Republic until 1945.

Anti-fascist movements began in the 1920s. After the defeat of the Axis the Nuremberg Trials convicted several Nazi leaders, and fascism has been almost universally condemned. George Orwell wrote in 1944 that the word had become almost meaningless.
fatehpur-sikri: The city takes its name from the village of Sikri, which occupied the site before. Excavations at Birchhabili Tila show a settlement from the 6th century CE and Jain temples of the 9th to 11th centuries. The Sikarwar Rajputs controlled the area from the 7th to the 16th century, until the Battle of Khanwa in 1527. Babur loved the place, called it Shukri, and laid out a garden there after defeating Rana Sangha.

Akbar had no surviving heir until 1569, when his son, later known as Jahangir, was born at Sikri. The Chishti saint Sheikh Salim had predicted the birth, and Akbar began a religious compound in his honour. After Jahangir's second birthday he started on a walled city and imperial palace. The city became known as Fatehpur Sikri, the City of Victory, after his Gujarat campaign of 1573. He left it in 1585 for a campaign in Punjab, and it was completely abandoned by 1610. The usual explanation is the failure of the water supply, though Akbar's loss of interest may also have played a part. After occupying Agra in 1803 the East India Company set up an administrative centre there, which remained until 1850.

The palace city stands on a rocky ridge about 3 kilometres long and 1 kilometre wide, enclosed by a wall some 6 kilometres long on three sides, with a lake on the fourth. Its architecture is modelled on Timurid forms, with Gujarati influences, and reflects both Hindu and Muslim domestic building of the time. Its continuous pattern of gardens and services leads archaeologists to conclude that it was built mainly to provide leisure and luxury for its residents.

The Jama Masjid was finished by 1571 to 1572, and the Buland Darwaza was added about five years later as a victory arch for the Gujarat campaign. The white marble tomb of Salim Chishti stands in the mosque's courtyard. The Diwan-i-Khas is known for its carved central pillar, and the Ibadat Khana, built in 1575, is where tradition says the foundations of Akbar's new syncretic faith, Din-e-Ilahi, were laid.

Because of its importance as a Mughal capital and its outstanding architecture, Fatehpur Sikri was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The state of preservation of its original spaces allows archaeologists to reconstruct scenes of Mughal court life. The town lies in the Agra District of Uttar Pradesh, about 37 kilometres from Agra.
fath-ali-shah-qajar: Fath-Ali Shah was born on 5 August 1772 at Damghan, where his father, Hossein Qoli Khan Qajar, was governor. Until his coronation he was known mainly as Baba Khan. His father was killed by the Kuklan Turkmens in 1777, and his uncle Agha Mohammad Khan, who married his mother, became his guardian. After Agha Mohammad Khan took the throne at Tehran on 21 March 1786, Baba Khan was named his heir and vice-regent. He was governor of Fars when his uncle was assassinated in 1797.

Baba Khan ascended the throne at Shiraz on 28 July 1797 and held his official coronation at Tehran on 19 March 1798. His coins bore his own name rather than a Shia Imam's, a sign of full sovereignty. The reign saw a revival of Persian arts and an elaborate court with rigid etiquette, with portraiture and oil painting reaching a height unknown under earlier Islamic dynasties thanks to his patronage. He also had rock reliefs carved beside those of the Sasanian Empire, presenting himself as heir to ancient Persia.

Russia took control of Georgia, which Iran had ruled intermittently since 1555, and in 1804 the shah went to war, under pressure from the Shia clergy. Russian artillery gave the advantage, and Britain and France both failed to support Iran. After the fall of Lankaran on 1 January 1813 he accepted the Treaty of Gulistan, which gave Russia Georgia and most khanates of the Caucasus. In 1826 he tried to recover them, and his son Abbas Mirza regained much ground at first. But Ivan Paskevich captured Erivan on 1 October 1827, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 gave Russia the khanates of Erivan and Nakhchivan, imposed a payment of 10 million in gold and provided for the resettlement of Armenians from Iran.

When the crown prince Abbas Mirza died on 25 October 1833, Fath-Ali Shah named his grandson Mohammed Mirza as heir. He died a year later and was buried in the shrine of Fatima Masumeh at Qom. Iranians often see him as a weak ruler because of the two treaties. Others stress that he turned a largely Turkic tribal khanship into a centralised monarchy on the old imperial model. He is recognisable in all of his 25 known portraits by his black beard, which reached below his waist, and he was survived by fifty-seven sons and forty-six daughters.
fatima: Fatima was born in Mecca to Khadija, the first of the Prophet Muhammad's wives. The mainstream Sunni view is that she was born in 605, five years before the first Quranic revelations, while Twelver sources report about 612 or 615. She is commonly called al-Zahra, the radiant, which the Shia take to refer to her creation from light, and hadith collections including Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim call her mistress of the women of paradise.

She married Muhammad's cousin Ali in Medina around 1 or 2 AH (623–5 CE), possibly after the Battle of Badr. Some companions, including Abu Bakr and Umar, had asked for her hand and been refused, since Muhammad said he was waiting for the moment fixed by destiny. When Muhammad put Ali's proposal to her she remained silent, which was understood as agreement, and on this report a woman's consent has always been needed in Islamic law.

Fatima was severely bereaved when Muhammad died in 11 AH, 632 CE. According to Shia tradition she contested Abu Bakr's succession and held that Ali was the rightful successor, and the village of Fadak near Medina was at issue between them, the Shia holding that Muhammad had given his share of it to her. She died within six months of her father. Sunnis believe she died of grief, while Shia Islam holds that injuries in a raid by Umar on her house caused a miscarriage and her death shortly after. According to the Sunni al-Tabari her dying wish was that Abu Bakr should not attend her funeral, and Ali buried her secretly at night, hiding the grave.

She was survived by her sons Hasan and Husayn, the second and third Shia imams, and her daughters Zaynab and Umm Kulthum. Her descendants bear the titles sayyid or sharif and are respected by Muslims. The Fatimid dynasty, which ruled in North Africa from 909 to 1171, claimed descent from her through the Isma'ili imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il, though the claim has been challenged. She is not named in the Quran, but commentaries link several verses to her, and Shia Islam limits the Ahl al-Bayt, the people of the house, to Muhammad, Fatima, Ali, Hasan and Husayn. She has been compared to Mary, mother of Jesus, especially in Shia Islam.
fatimid-caliphate: The Fatimids led Isma'ilism, a revolutionary Shi'a movement that was at once political and religious, philosophical and social, and that originally proclaimed the arrival of an Islamic messiah. They traced their descent from Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad, and her husband Ali, and called themselves simply the Alid dynasty. The origins of the movement are obscure before the late ninth century. Its founder, Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah, was Arab in origin, but its first army was made up of Kutama Berbers from Little Kabylia.

Ifriqiya was then held by the Aghlabids, an Arab dynasty that ruled nominally for the Abbasids. In 893 the missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i settled among the Kutama, and over two years he won most of the tribes by persuasion or coercion and set up an Isma'ili theocratic state at Tazrut, near Mila. Between 902 and 909 his forces conquered Aghlabid Ifriqiya, and al-Mahdi was accepted as imam and first caliph in 909.

For much of the tenth century the Fatimids rivalled the Umayyads of Córdoba for control of the western Maghreb. Their capitals were first al-Mahdiyya, on a peninsula on the coast of modern Tunisia, then al-Mansuriyya near Kairouan. In 969 the general Jawhar invaded Egypt, which the Ikhshidids held, and founded al-Qahira, Cairo, several miles north-east of Fustat. The caliphate's centre moved there in 973, and Egypt became the political, cultural and religious centre of the empire.

After the reigns of al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, the long reign of al-Mustansir left the caliph aloof from affairs and the viziers more powerful. Factionalism in the army led to a civil war in the 1060s, followed by a revival under the vizier Badr al-Jamali. The Seljuk Turks pressed into Syria in the 1070s and the Crusaders arrived in the Levant in 1097. In 1171 Saladin abolished the dynasty and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. After al-Mustansir his sons Nizar and al-Musta'li both claimed the imamate, splitting the Isma'ilis into Nizari and Musta'li branches.

Fatimid society was highly pluralistic. Isma'ili Shi'ism was the religion of the state and the court, but most Muslims stayed Sunni, a large part of the population remained Christian, and Jews were a smaller minority. Non-Muslims were dhimmis and paid the jizya, and scholars generally agree that Fatimid rule was tolerant and inclusive. Its leaders made little headway in persuading the population to adopt their beliefs.

The army began with Kutama Berbers. From the reign of al-'Aziz Turkish freedmen, Daylamis, Kurds and Black infantry bought as slaves in Nubia joined it, and the Kutama lost their privileged place. Fatimid art is known for lively figurative motifs, angular floriated Kufic script, lustre ceramics and carved rock crystal. The mosque of al-Azhar in Cairo still stands.
fatwa: A fatwa is a legal ruling on a point of Islamic law given by a qualified jurist, or faqih, in answer to a question from a private person, a judge or a government. The jurist who issues it is a mufti, and the act is called ifta. The word comes from an Arabic root with meanings that include youth, newness and clarification. The practice has roots in the Quran, which on several occasions tells Muhammad how to answer questions from his followers, in two cases with verbal forms of the root f-t-y.

After Muhammad's death in 632 the community turned to his Companions for guidance, and then to the generation of Successors, and the question-and-answer format took its definitive form with the development of the classical theory of Islamic law.

Fatwas are issued in reply to a query and may range from a yes or no answer to a book-length treatise. Queries were supposed to concern real situations and to leave out names of places and people. A fatwa is nonbinding, unless issued by a government judge in an Islamic state, whereas a court decision is binding. It may deal with rituals, ethics, doctrine and sometimes philosophy, and it applies to every case fitting the premises of the question, while a judgment applies only to its own case. The classical institution resembles the jus respondendi of Roman law and the responsa of Jewish law.

Fatwas played three roles in the classical legal system: they informed Muslims about ritual and ethics, advised courts on finer points of law, and developed substantive law, since author-jurists collected the fatwas of prominent muftis in books. Manuals called adab al-mufti required a mufti to be an adult Muslim of good character and sound mind, trained as a jurist. A student normally studied for several years with recognised scholars, and a teacher certified readiness to issue fatwas with an ijaza. Over the centuries Sunni muftis were gradually incorporated into state bureaucracies, while Shia jurists in Iran asserted autonomous authority from the early modern era.

Public and political fatwas were issued to take a stand on doctrinal controversies, to legitimise government policies or to express grievances, and during European colonialism they helped mobilise resistance. In the modern era codified state laws and Western-style legal education displaced muftis from elaborating the law applied in courts, and fatwas increasingly advise the public on ritual and everyday life.
fayzabad-badakhshan: Fayzabad stands on the right bank of the Kokcha River, near where the river leaves a gorge and before it reaches a large open plain, at an altitude of 1,254 metres. Historically it connected Kabul with Kashgar in Xinjiang, China, and it is the main commercial and administrative centre of the Pamir region. Its bazaars trade cotton cloth, salt, sugar, tea, indigo and cutlery. Barley, wheat and rice are grown around it, and gold is panned and salt mined nearby. Before the 21st century the town was relatively isolated from the rest of Afghanistan for lack of paved roads.

Until 1680 the town was called Jauz Gun because of the many walnut farms in the area (jauz means walnut). It was renamed Faizabad, roughly the abode of divine bounty, blessing and charity, when the robe of the Prophet Muhammad was delivered there. Tradition holds that Muhammad Shaykh Ziya and Shaykh Niyaz brought it after Wais Qaran had carried it to Balkh. The city then replaced Munjan as the capital of Badakhshan. The relic was removed to Kandahar by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1768, who established the Kirka Sharif there. Seven historical forts, several now in ruins, were built in and around the city to defend it and the road in and out.

In 1821 Mohammad Murad Beg destroyed the city and its inhabitants were removed to Kunduz. After Emir Abdur Rahman Khan annexed it in 1888 the town regained its former importance and became a considerable place of trade. In 1979 it became a base of Afghan mujahideen resisting the Soviet invasion, and Soviet forces took it in 1980 and made it one of their bases in Afghanistan.

Fayzabad is the capital of Badakhshan Province, with an estimated population of 85,477, mostly Tajiks, with Pashtun, Pamiri, Uzbek, Hazara and Turkmen communities. Eleven languages are spoken there, among them Dari, Pashto, Wakhi, Shughni and Uzbek. It is home to Badakhshan University and serves as the gateway to the Wakhan National Park in Wakhan District.
february-revolution: The revolution took place when Russia still used the Julian calendar, which is why it is called the February Revolution although its events fell in March by the Gregorian calendar. Historians disagree about its main causes. Liberal historians stress the turmoil of the First World War, Marxists the inevitability of change, and revisionists land disputes after the end of serfdom. Long-term causes included the failure of Imperial Russia to modernise its structures while keeping loyalty to the autocracy, and the Revolution of 1905.

By early 1917 the Russian army had suffered about 9.15 million casualties, including some 1.7 million killed, and desertion ran at around 34,000 a month. The authority of Nicholas II was further weakened by the assassination of Rasputin on 30 December 1916 and by a rapid turnover of ministers.

Workers at the Putilov Factory went on strike on 18 February Old Style (3 March New Style). On 23 February Old Style (8 March) they were joined by women marking International Women's Day and protesting against food rationing. By the next day nearly 200,000 protesters were in the streets, and by 25 February some 250,000 were on strike and nearly all industrial enterprises in Petrograd had shut down.

Many soldiers of the garrison, largely draftees of low morale, joined the crowds, and on 27 February Old Style most of it sided with the revolutionaries. Duma members formed a Provisional Committee, and the socialist parties re-established the Petrograd Soviet. The committee took control of the railway telegraph and forbade trains to travel within 265 kilometres of Petrograd, which made it very hard for loyal troops to reach the capital. Nicholas II, stranded on his train at Pskov, was forced to abdicate on the advice of his generals. Over 1,300 people were killed.

A Provisional Government, at first under Georgy Lvov, replaced the Council of Ministers. Its manifesto promised civil and political rights and a Constituent Assembly but did not address the war or land. It shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet in an arrangement known as dual power; the Soviet had more practical power because it controlled the workers and soldiers.

After the July Days, in which the government killed hundreds of protesters, Alexander Kerensky became head of the government. He could not resolve food shortages and mass unemployment and kept Russia in the war. These failures led to the October Revolution by the Bolsheviks, and the collapse of authority contributed to the Russian Civil War and the formation of the Soviet Union.
federalism: The words federalism and confederalism share a root in the Latin foedus, meaning treaty, pact or covenant. Until the late eighteenth century they meant much the same thing, a simple league among sovereign states based on a treaty. The first forms of federalism were alliances between tribes or city states in ancient times, such as the Delian League. The Achaean League of Hellenistic Greece is considered an early ancestor, since cities then banded together even at the cost of surrendering part of their sovereignty. Johannes Althusius is considered the father of modern federalism, along with Montesquieu, and in the modern era it was first adopted by a union of states of the Old Swiss Confederacy from the mid-14th century.

Federalism combines a general level of government with a regional level of sub-unit governments, such as states, provinces or cantons, and divides the powers of governing between them. It differs from confederalism, where the central government is subordinate to the regional states, and from the unitary state, where the regional level is subordinate to the centre. James Madison called the new United States Constitution neither a national nor a federal constitution, but a composition of both, and in the nineteenth century federalism in the United States came to mean this new compound form alone.

In a federation the division of power is usually set out in the constitution, and the right of the component states to self-government is entrenched. Foreign policy and defence are almost always federal powers. An upper house often represents the component states, as in the Senate of the United States and Australia and the German Bundesrat. Constitutional amendment often requires the consent of the states.

Proponents have argued that the checks and the sharing of power in a federation reduce threats from within and abroad and allow a state to be both large and diverse. The word has opposite senses on two continents. In the United States the Federalists of the founding era wanted a stronger central government, while in Europe federalists favour a common government above the nations, an idea that grew out of post-war Europe and Winston Churchill's speech in Zürich in 1946. Anarchists such as Pierre-Joseph Proudhon envisaged a stateless federalism built from the bottom up.
federated-states-of-micronesia: The Federated States of Micronesia consists of around 607 islands spread across the western Pacific just north of the equator, with a combined land area of about 702 square kilometres. It includes most of the Caroline Islands, excluding Palau. Each of the four states, Yap, Chuuk (called Truk until January 1990), Pohnpei (Ponape until November 1984) and Kosrae (formerly Kusaie), is centred on one or more main volcanic islands, and all but Kosrae include numerous outlying atolls. The climate is warm, humid and rainy all year round.

The ancestors of the Micronesians settled more than four thousand years ago. A decentralised chieftain-based system eventually evolved into a more centralised economic and religious culture centred on Yap. On Pohnpei, Nan Madol, a series of small artificial islands linked by canals and often called the Venice of the Pacific, was the ceremonial and political seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, which united the island's estimated 25,000 people from about 500 CE until the centralised system collapsed around 1500.

The Portuguese and then the Spanish reached the Carolines in the sixteenth century, and Spain incorporated the archipelago into the Spanish East Indies. When Germany began extending its influence in the 1870s, Pope Leo XIII was asked in the Carolines Question of 1885 to decide between the two powers, and he confirmed Spanish authority while giving Germany free access. After its defeat in the Spanish–American War, Spain sold the archipelago to Germany in 1899. Japan captured it in the First World War and administered it under a League of Nations mandate.

In February 1944 the United States Navy attacked the Japanese base at Truk Lagoon in Operation Hailstone, sinking numerous ships and destroying hundreds of aircraft. In 1947 the islands became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States. On 10 May 1979 four districts ratified a constitution, and the Compact of Free Association with the United States entered into force on 3 November 1986. The United Nations ended the trusteeship in 1990.

The capital is Palikir on Pohnpei, and the largest city is Weno in the Chuuk Lagoon. English is the official language of the federation, and 17 other languages are spoken. Yap is known for its stone money, large calcite disks called Rai stones, and Nan Madol is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
felix-dzerzhinsky: Felix Edmundovich Dzerzhinsky was born on 11 September 1877 on the Ozhyemblovo estate near Ivyanets, in the Minsk Governorate of Russian Poland, now Belarus, to Polish parents of old noble descent. His father, a teacher, died of tuberculosis in 1882. He attended the Vilnius Gymnasium from 1887 and was expelled shortly before graduating for revolutionary activity. In 1895 he had joined a Marxist group, and he later helped found the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland and Lithuania, which took the position of Rosa Luxemburg on the right of nations to self-determination.

He was arrested for the first time in 1897 and served almost a year in Kaunas prison. Exiled to Siberia several times, he escaped every time, and he worked for his party in Berlin, where he met Luxemburg. After the failed Revolution of 1905 he was jailed again. The police found him at the end of 1912, and he spent four and a half years in prison, where Russian guards beat him, disfiguring his jaw and mouth. The February Revolution of 1917 freed him from Butyrka prison.

He joined the Bolsheviks, entered the Central Committee in July 1917 and took part in the October Revolution. On 20 December 1917 the Council of People's Commissars established the Cheka, with Dzerzhinsky as its director. It became notorious for mass summary executions, and tens of thousands of political opponents and saboteurs were shot without trial in prison basements and public places during the Red Terror. Dzerzhinsky said, We represent in ourselves organized terror. In 1922 the Cheka became the GPU and in 1923 the OGPU, with Dzerzhinsky still at its head.

Dzerzhinsky died of a heart attack on 20 July 1926, immediately after a two-hour speech denouncing the United Opposition of Leon Trotsky, Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev. He was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis and succeeded at the OGPU by Vyacheslav Menzhinsky. Chekists remembered him as a hero of the revolution, and many places in the Soviet Union were named after him, while critics saw him as a symbol of repression and brutality. The iron statue sculpted by Yevgeny Vuchetich in 1958 stood on Lubyanka Square near the KGB headquarters, known as Iron Felix. The Moscow Soviet had it removed in August 1991 after the failed coup attempt.
felix-houphouet-boigny: According to his official biography Houphouët-Boigny was probably born on 18 October 1905 in Yamoussoukro, into a family of hereditary chiefs of the Baoulé people; unofficial accounts place his birth up to seven years earlier. After the village chief Kouassi N'Go was murdered in 1910, he was named his successor, and his stepfather ruled as regent. In 1925 he began work as a doctor's aide at a hospital in Abidjan. At Abengourou he saw the mistreatment of African cocoa farmers by colonists, and in 1932 he led a movement of farmers against the large white landowners.

As chef de canton of Akouè he took charge of the family plantation and became one of Africa's richest farmers. On 3 September 1944 he founded the African Agricultural Union, which demanded better working conditions and the abolition of forced labour. Elected to the French National Assembly in 1945, he proposed a bill to abolish forced labour, adopted on 11 April 1946 as the Loi Houphouët-Boigny. In October 1946 he helped found the African Democratic Rally at Bamako and became its president. From 1956 he was a minister in the French government, the first African in so senior a post.

He became head of the government of Ivory Coast on 1 May 1959 and was elected unopposed president on 27 November 1960, after independence on 7 August 1960. The constitution he drafted gave great power to the executive. He kept the closest links with France, a policy he called Françafrique, and severed relations with the Soviet Union in 1969, restoring them in February 1986. His liberal economic laws of 1959 encouraged foreign investors, and the economy grew by 11 to 12 percent a year from 1960 to 1965.

From 1978 the fall in world prices of coffee and cocoa brought a serious decline. Houphouët-Boigny delayed naming a successor, and by 1990 Prime Minister Alassane Ouattara was running the country while the president was in hospital in France. He died of prostate cancer on 7 December 1993 and left no written will. A contest between Henri Konan Bédié, president of the National Assembly, and Ouattara followed, and Ouattara resigned as prime minister on 9 December. In 1989 he had created a peace prize sponsored by UNESCO. He also moved the capital from Abidjan to Yamoussoukro and built the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace there.
feminism: Feminist movements originated in late 18th-century Europe. Mary Wollstonecraft is seen by many as a founder of feminism because of her book A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), in which she argues that class and private property are the basis of discrimination against women, and that women as much as men needed equal rights.

The word came later. Charles Fourier is credited with coining féminisme in 1837, but no trace of the word has been found in his works. It first appeared in France in 1871, in a medical thesis by Ferdinand-Valère Faneau de la Cour, and Alexandre Dumas fils coined féministe in 1872 for men who supported women's rights; both uses were very negative. The Oxford English Dictionary dates its first appearance in English in this meaning to 1895.

Feminism is a range of movements and ideologies that aim to establish the political, economic, personal and social equality of the sexes. It holds that modern societies are patriarchal and that women are treated unjustly in them. Since the 19th century, first-wave liberal feminism, which sought political and legal equality through reforms within a liberal democratic framework, was contrasted with labour-based proletarian women's movements that developed into socialist and Marxist feminism. Since the 1960s both have been contrasted with radical feminism, which arose from the radical wing of second-wave feminism.

Feminist theory emerged from the movements and draws on anthropology, sociology, economics, literary criticism, psychoanalysis and philosophy to understand gender inequality. In the 1970s French feminists such as Hélène Cixous developed the concept of écriture féminine, or female writing.

Many scholars consider feminist campaigns a main force behind changes in women's rights, particularly in the West, where they are near-universally credited with women's suffrage, reproductive rights and the right to enter into contracts and own property. At the International Conference of Socialist Women in Stuttgart in 1907, suffrage was described as a tool of class struggle. In 1918 Constance Markievicz became the first woman elected to the British House of Commons, but in line with Sinn Féin policy she did not take her seat. In the United States the National Organization for Women began in 1966 to seek equality, including through the Equal Rights Amendment, which did not pass.
feodor-chaliapin: Feodor Chaliapin was born on 1 February 1873 (Old Style) in Kazan and baptised the next day at the Epiphany Cathedral. His father, Ivan Yakovlevich, was a clerk in the district council, and in 1878 the family moved to the village of Ametyevo, now part of Kazan. His vocal teacher was Dmitri Usatov. Chaliapin began his career in Tbilisi and at the Imperial Opera in Saint Petersburg in 1894, and then sang at the Mamontov Private Opera from 1896 to 1899.

At the Mamontov Opera he met Sergei Rachmaninoff, then an assistant conductor, who remained a lifelong friend. Rachmaninoff taught him to analyse a score and insisted that he learn all the roles of an opera, and together they prepared the title role of Modest Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov.

In 1901 he made a debut at La Scala as the devil in Arrigo Boito's Mefistofele under Arturo Toscanini, who later called him the finest talent he had worked with. His first Metropolitan Opera season, in 1907, was disappointing because audiences found the frankness of his acting shocking. He returned in 1921 and sang there for eight seasons. In 1913 the impresario Sergei Diaghilev introduced him to London and Paris, where he also gave recitals of Russian folk songs, among them The Song of the Volga Boatmen.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917 he was at first treated as a revered artist, but the difficulties of life under the new regime and the Civil War, and reportedly the seizure of some of his property, led him to stay outside Russia after 1921. He lived first in Finland and then in France, with Paris as his base. He made one sound film, G. W. Pabst's Don Quixote of 1933, and published the memoir Man and Mask in 1932. His last stage performance was as Boris Godunov at the Monte Carlo Opera in 1937.

He died of leukaemia in Paris and was buried at the Batignolles cemetery until 1984, when his remains were moved to the Novodevichy cemetery in Moscow. Largely through his advocacy, Russian operas such as Khovanshchina, Prince Igor and Sadko became known in the West.
feodor-i-of-russia: Feodor was born in Moscow on 31 May 1557, the third son of Ivan IV by his first wife Anastasia Romanovna. His mother died when he was three, and he grew up in the shadow of a distant father with only one surviving older brother, Ivan Ivanovich. He was sickly and diffident, extremely pious, and fond of visiting churches and having the bells rung, which earned him the name Feodor the Bellringer. In 1575 he married Irina Godunova, sister of the minister Boris Godunov. Ivan Ivanovich died on 9 November 1581, leaving Feodor and the infant Dmitry as the only sons.

Ivan IV died in March 1584, and Feodor was crowned tsar and autocrat of all Russia in the Dormition Cathedral in Moscow on 31 May 1584. Historians have debated whether an assembly, the Zemsky Sobor, elected him; the few contemporary Russian sources say only that he took the throne by his father's blessing. Feodor was the nominal ruler. Boris Godunov acted as de facto regent, and by the end of the 1580s he dealt with foreign powers independently. Irina also took some part in affairs, and three charters to monasteries between 1587 and 1597 are in the names of both tsar and tsaritsa.

In May 1586 the Shuysky family petitioned in the name of the Zemsky Sobor for Feodor to divorce his childless wife. He refused. The Shuyskys were banished from the capital and Godunov persecuted them heavily the following year. In foreign affairs Feodor declared the country open to all foreigners instead of keeping exclusive trading rights for England, and dismissed the English ambassador Sir Jerome Bowes. Elizabeth I sent Giles Fletcher the Elder to protest, without success.

Irina bore a daughter, Feodosiya, in 1592, after almost twelve years of marriage; the child died in 1594 aged two. Feodor died in Moscow on 17 January 1598 and was buried in the Archangel Cathedral in the Kremlin. After forty days of mourning the Zemsky Sobor elected Godunov tsar. Feodor's death ended the central branch of the Rurik dynasty, and the end of the line was later followed by the Time of Troubles. Contemporaries described his reign as a time of prosperity and stability, though much of the credit went to Godunov. Feodor was venerated soon after his death and is listed in the Great Synaxaristes of the Orthodox Church.
feodor-iii-of-russia: Feodor was born in Moscow on 9 June 1661, the eldest surviving son of Tsar Alexis and Maria Miloslavskaya, and he succeeded his father in 1676 at the age of fifteen. He was educated by Simeon Polotsky, the most learned Slavonic monk of the day, and knew Polish and Latin. He had been disabled from birth, however, and was half paralysed by a mysterious illness, supposedly scurvy. He spent most of his time with young nobles, Ivan Maksimovich Yazykov and Aleksei Timofeievich Likhachov.

On 28 July 1680 Feodor married a noblewoman, Agaphia Simeonovna Grushevskaya, and took up the sceptre. He proved a devoted reformer. The atmosphere of the court became less oppressive and the severity of the penal laws was considerably reduced. He founded an academy in the Zaikonospassky monastery, where professors were to teach everything not expressly forbidden by the Orthodox church, including Slavonic, Greek, Latin and Polish. A household census took place in 1678.

His most notable reform, made at the suggestion of Vasily Galitzine, was the abolition in 1682 of mestnichestvo, or place priority, which had paralysed the civil and military administration of the Tsardom for generations. From then on appointments were to be made by merit and by the will of the sovereign, and the pedigree books were to be destroyed. Agaphia shared his progressive views and was the first to advocate beard-shaving.

On 11 July 1681 Agaphia gave birth to a son, Tsarevich Ilya Fyodorovich, the expected heir. She died three days later, on 14 July, and the child died on 21 July. On 24 February 1682 Feodor married Marfa Apraksina; he was so weak that he could not stand at the wedding. He died on 7 May 1682, three months after it, without surviving issue, and the news of his death sparked the Moscow Uprising of 1682.
feodosia: Greek colonists from Miletos founded Theodosia in the 6th century BCE. Its trade depended on rich agricultural lands, and it was destroyed by the Huns in the 4th century CE. For much of the next nine hundred years it was a minor village, at times within the sphere of influence of the Khazars and of the Byzantine Empire, and it was conquered by the Mongols in the 1230s.

In the late 13th century traders from the Republic of Genoa bought the city from the Golden Horde. Their settlement, Kaffa, virtually monopolised trade in the Black Sea region and housed one of Europe's biggest slave markets. Ibn Battuta described a wonderful harbour with about two hundred vessels, and in 1318 Pope John XXII established a Latin diocese of Kaffa. It is believed that the Black Death entered Europe through Kaffa in 1347, after a siege in which the Mongol army under Jani Beg reportedly catapulted infected corpses over the walls. The plague appears to have spread step by step, and other Crimean ports and overland routes may also have carried it.

In 1475 an Ottoman fleet under Gedik Ahmet Pasha anchored before the city on 1 June, began bombarding it the next day, and received its surrender on 6 June. The Ottomans took the inhabitants' wealth, abducted 1,500 youths for the sultan's palace, and on 8 July ordered all inhabitants of Latin origin to move to Istanbul. In 1616 Zaporozhian Cossacks under Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny destroyed the Turkish fleet, captured the city and freed the slaves. Russia took over Crimea between 1774 and 1783, and the city became Feodosia.

Feodosia is a resort city on the Black Sea coast of Crimea, with beaches, mineral springs and mud baths. Its Golden Beach, made of small seashells, stretches for some 15 kilometres. The painter Ivan Aivazovsky lived and worked there all his life, and the Aivazovsky National Art Gallery and the Genoese fortress are among its best-known sights.
ferdinand-de-lesseps: Ferdinand de Lesseps was born at Versailles on 19 November 1805 into a family of diplomats; his father Mathieu de Lesseps was in the consular service. Through his father he came to know Muhammad Ali, the ruler of Egypt, and Muhammad Ali's son Sa'id, who became his friend. His own diplomatic career began in Lisbon in 1825 and took him to Tunis, Alexandria, Cairo, Rotterdam, Málaga and Barcelona. In Alexandria he read a memoir on the abandoned ancient canal at Suez, which helped give him the idea of a canal across the isthmus. Recalled in 1849 after a mission to Rome, he left the diplomatic service.

When Sa'id Pasha became viceroy of Egypt in 1854, Lesseps landed at Alexandria on 7 November, and on 30 November the viceroy signed a concession authorizing him to oversee the French portion of the Suez Canal's construction. British opposition, including that of Lord Palmerston, did not deter him. French subscribers supplied more than half of the capital of two hundred million francs, and the Egyptian government took shares worth eighty million francs. The first blow of the pickaxe was struck at Port Said on 25 April 1859, and the canal was opened on 17 November 1869 by the Khedive Ismail Pasha.

A congress of 136 delegates in Paris in May 1879 voted for a Panama canal without locks, like Suez, and Lesseps, aged 74, became president of the company. Work began in 1882 but was dogged by landslides and by deaths from malaria and yellow fever. The Panama Canal Company declared itself bankrupt in December 1888 and entered liquidation in February 1889.

The failure became known as the Panama Canal Scandal after it emerged by 1892 that 150 French deputies had been bribed to vote the company financial aid. In February 1893 Lesseps, his son Charles and others were tried and found guilty. Lesseps was fined and sentenced to prison, but the Court of Cassation overturned the prison sentence because more than three years had passed since the offence. In 1904 the United States bought the company's assets and resumed work on a revised plan. Lesseps died in Indre on 7 December 1894 and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery.
ferdinand-i-holy-roman-emperor: Ferdinand was born on 10 March 1503 at Alcalá de Henares in Castile, the second son of Philip I of Castile and Joanna of Castile. After his father's death in 1506 his maternal grandfather Ferdinand II of Aragon, with whom he shared a name and a birthday, became his guardian, and he was raised in the royal household with an education in literature, the sciences and languages. He grew up as a patron of the arts and of scholars. He did not learn German until he was a young adult.

When Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia was killed at Mohács on 29 August 1526, Ferdinand at once declared himself a candidate. On 24 October 1526 the Bohemian Diet elected him king of Bohemia on condition that he confirm the estates' privileges, but it refused to recognise him as hereditary ruler. In Hungary a Diet of the lesser nobility proclaimed John Zápolya, Voivode of Transylvania, king on 10 November 1526, and Ferdinand, supported by Charles V, held the western part, which became known as Royal Hungary.

In 1547 Ferdinand defeated a Protestant revolt in Bohemia, after which he centralised its administration and revoked many urban privileges. At the Diet of Augsburg of 1555, with authority from Charles to act and settle, he brought the delegates to agree on the principle of cuius regio, eius religio. He rushed one article through the debate and added the Declaratio Ferdinandei at the last minute, and these became flaws in the settlement. Charles abdicated in August 1556, and Ferdinand succeeded him as emperor. He founded the Hofkriegsrat in 1556 to coordinate military affairs in all Habsburg lands, but the governments of Austria, Bohemia and Hungary stayed distinct.

In December 1562 Ferdinand had his eldest son Maximilian elected King of the Romans. Ferdinand died in Vienna in 1564 and was buried in Prague. Historians describe him as a mediocre military commander but an energetic and imaginative administrator, whose framework for his lands endured into the eighteenth century. Some historians hold that he was nearly the closest the Holy Roman Empire came to a Protestant emperor, while others hold that he was as Catholic as his brother but saw religion as outside politics.
ferdinand-i-of-austria: Ferdinand was the eldest son of Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Maria Theresa of Naples and Sicily. His parents were double first cousins, sharing all four grandparents, so that he descended twice from each of his four great-grandparents. Possibly as a result of this closeness, he had hydrocephalus, neurological problems including epilepsy, and a speech impediment. He was educated by Baron Josef Kalasanz von Erberg and his wife, Countess Josephine von Attems. He married Maria Anna of Savoy, the sixth child of Victor Emmanuel I of Sardinia, and the couple had no children.

Ferdinand succeeded his father Francis I on 2 March 1835 as Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary, where he was Ferdinand V, and ruler of the other lands of the Habsburg monarchy. He was also president of the German Confederation until 12 July 1848. Because of severe epilepsy he was thought unable to rule, and his father's will told him to consult his uncle Archduke Louis on internal policy and urged him to be guided by Prince Metternich, the foreign minister. Although he was never declared incapacitated, a Regent's Council of Archduke Louis, Count Kolowrat and Metternich steered the government.

Later accounts have depicted him as feeble-minded, yet he kept a coherent and legible diary and is said to have had a sharp wit. He suffered as many as twenty seizures a day, which severely limited his ability to govern. His good nature earned him the nickname The Benign in Austria and, in Bohemia, the Czech form Ferdinand Dobrotivý. He was the last King of Bohemia to be crowned as such and the last ruler crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy as King of Lombardy-Venetia.

When the revolutionaries of 1848 marched on the palace, Ferdinand is supposed to have asked Metternich what was happening and, on hearing that a revolution had begun, to have replied, "But are they allowed to do that?" Prince Felix of Schwarzenberg persuaded him to abdicate in favour of his nephew Franz Joseph. The next in line, his brother Franz Karl, renounced his rights in favour of his son at his wife Sophie's urging. Ferdinand abdicated on 2 December 1848, and Franz Joseph reigned for the next 68 years. In his diary he described the new emperor kneeling for his blessing. He lived in Hradčany Palace in Prague until his death on 29 June 1875, and is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna.
ferdinand-i-of-bulgaria: Ferdinand was born in Vienna on 26 February 1861, the son of Prince August of Saxe-Coburg and Clémentine of Orléans, a daughter of King Louis Philippe I of France. He was raised a Catholic in the high nobility of Austria-Hungary and served as an officer in the Austro-Hungarian Army. The House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha held several European thrones in the 19th century, and Ferdinand himself founded the royal dynasty of Bulgaria.

Alexander of Battenberg had abdicated in 1886 after a pro-Russian coup, and the Grand National Assembly elected Ferdinand prince on 7 July 1887. Queen Victoria thought him unfit, but he generally gave a good account of himself in his first two decades. After the fall of the minister Stefan Stambolov in 1894, Ferdinand had his infant son Boris converted to Orthodoxy in 1896, restoring relations with Russia, and was excommunicated by Pope Leo XIII. On 5 October 1908 he proclaimed Bulgaria's independence from the Ottoman Empire and took the title of tsar, at the Church of the Holy Forty Martyrs in Tarnovo.

In 1912 Bulgaria joined Greece, Montenegro and Serbia against the Ottomans, and the Bulgarian army took Adrianople on 13 March 1913. Disputes over the division of Macedonia led to the Second Balkan War, in which Bulgaria was defeated, though the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913 gave it Western Thrace and access to the Aegean. On 11 October 1915 Bulgaria attacked Serbia after a treaty with Austria-Hungary and Germany. After military setbacks in 1918, Ferdinand abdicated in favour of his eldest son, who became Tsar Boris III on 3 October 1918.

Ferdinand married Princess Marie Louise of Bourbon-Parma in 1893; she died in 1899 after the birth of their fourth child, and he married Princess Eleonore Reuss of Köstritz in 1908. After his abdication he lived in Coburg, spending time on gardening, travel and natural history. He lived to see his son Boris III die in 1943, the monarchy end in 1946 and his son Kyril executed. He died in Coburg on 10 September 1948 and was buried in the family crypt there, since the communist authorities would not let him be buried in Bulgaria.
ferdinand-i-of-romania: Ferdinand was born on 24 August 1865 in Sigmaringen in south-western Germany, the second son of Leopold, Prince of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, and Infanta Antónia of Portugal. After his father renounced his rights in 1880 and his elder brother in 1886, he became heir presumptive to his childless uncle, King Carol I of Romania. In 1889 the Romanian parliament recognised him as a prince of Romania. He was allowed to remain a Catholic, but his children had to be raised Orthodox, and for agreeing to this he was excommunicated, though the sentence was later lifted. He married Princess Marie of Edinburgh, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, at Sigmaringen on 10 January 1893.

Ferdinand became king on 10 October 1914 after Carol I died without surviving children. Although he belonged to a cadet branch of the German ruling house, he led Romania into the First World War on the side of the Triple Entente on 27 August 1916, which earned him the nickname the Loyal, for keeping his oath to reign as a good Romanian. Emperor Wilhelm II had his name erased from the Hohenzollern register. After the Central Powers occupied Dobruja and Wallachia, Romania fought on in 1917 and stopped the German advance into Moldavia. When Russia made peace in 1918, Ferdinand refused to sign and ratify the Treaty of Bucharest.

Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania joined the Kingdom of Romania in 1918 to 1920. Ferdinand was crowned king of Greater Romania on 15 October 1922 at Alba Iulia, in the newly consecrated Coronation Cathedral. His reign saw agrarian reform and universal suffrage, and politics were dominated by the National Liberal Party of Ion and Vintilă Brătianu.

In December 1925 his eldest son Carol renounced his rights to the throne, causing a dynastic crisis, because the next in line was Carol's young son Michael. Ferdinand removed Carol's name from the royal house. He died of colon cancer at Sinaia on 20 July 1927 and was succeeded by his grandson Michael under a regency of three. He is known in Romania as the Unifier.
ferdinand-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Ferdinand was born in the castle at Graz on 9 July 1578, the son of Archduke Charles II and Maria of Bavaria, her husband's niece, whose marriage reconciled the two leading Catholic families of the Holy Roman Empire. His mother managed his education. In early 1590 he was sent to the Jesuit college at Ingolstadt in Bavaria, to keep him away from the Lutheran nobles of Styria. His father died on 10 July 1590, and Ferdinand inherited Inner Austria, with regents appointed by his cousin Emperor Rudolf II. He took over its government in 1596 and 1597.

Ferdinand was charged with defending Croatia, Slavonia and south-eastern Hungary against the Ottoman Empire. He regarded the regulation of religion as a royal prerogative and from 1598 ordered the expulsion of Protestant pastors and teachers and set up commissions to restore Catholic parishes. His attempt to retake the fortress of Nagykanizsa ended in defeat in November 1601. In the Brothers' Quarrel he first backed Matthias against Rudolf II, but Matthias's concessions to Protestants outraged him. In 1617 Philip III of Spain acknowledged his right to succeed Matthias in Bohemia and Hungary in return for territorial concessions.

The Bohemian estates confirmed Ferdinand as successor only after he promised to respect their privileges. Disputes over the Letter of Majesty, which set out the freedoms of Bohemian Protestants, led on 23 May 1618 to an uprising in Prague, when armed nobles threw two royal governors out of a window. After Matthias died on 20 March 1619, Ferdinand was elected Holy Roman Emperor at Frankfurt on 28 August 1619, and the Bohemian estates deposed him as king and offered the crown to the Calvinist Frederick V of the Palatinate.

The Thirty Years' War, which began in 1618, followed from the failures of Rudolf II and Matthias on one account, but Ferdinand's measures against Protestantism spread it through the whole empire. He aimed to make Catholicism the only religion of the empire. The war left the empire devastated, and its population did not recover until 1710.
ferdinand-ii-of-aragon: Ferdinand was born on 10 March 1452 in Sos del Rey Católico in the Kingdom of Aragon, the son of John II of Aragon, of a cadet branch of the House of Trastámara, by his second wife, Juana Enríquez. On 19 October 1469 he married Isabella, the half-sister and heir presumptive of Henry IV of Castile, in Valladolid. The two were second cousins, and they married under a clear prenuptial agreement on sharing power and the joint motto tanto monta, monta tanto. When Isabella succeeded her brother he became king of Castile through his wife, and the two had first to fight a civil war against the supporters of Joanna la Beltraneja, which they won swiftly.

When Ferdinand succeeded his father in 1479, the Crown of Castile and the territories of the Crown of Aragon were united in a personal union, as separate units under the same monarchs. Their early joint rule saw the completion in 1492 of the conquest of the Emirate of Granada. In March of that year they issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering all Jews to convert or leave, and they commissioned Christopher Columbus. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 divided the world beyond Europe between Portugal and Castile. In 1502 Ferdinand ended the religious freedom guaranteed to Muslims by the Treaty of Granada of 1491 and forced them to convert or leave.

The later part of his life was largely taken up with the Italian Wars against the kings of France. His general Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba won Naples from the French by 1504. After Isabella's death on 26 November 1504 Ferdinand became governor of Castile for their daughter Joanna, but the Castilian nobility rebuffed him and in the Treaty of Villafáfila of 1506 he gave way to her husband Philip. In 1506 he married Germaine of Foix. Philip's death in September 1506 returned him to power, and in 1507 he had Joanna confined and ruled Castile in her name. He took part in the League of Cambrai against Venice and the Holy League against Louis XII, and in 1512 he invaded Navarre.

Ferdinand died on 23 January 1516 at Madrigalejo in Extremadura, and is entombed at the Capilla Real in Granada, beside Isabella, Joanna and Philip. Joanna inherited Aragon and was nominally his successor, but power soon passed to her son Charles, who inherited the Spanish and Italian lands of his maternal grandparents as well as the Austrian and Burgundian lands of his father's family. The Catholic Monarchs centralised the crown's power, at least in name, and laid the groundwork for a formidable military. Legally, Castile and Aragon remained two kingdoms until the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 to 1716, though Ferdinand is considered the de facto first king of Spain.
ferdinand-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Ferdinand was born in Graz on 13 July 1608, the third son of Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Maria Anna of Bavaria, and was baptised Ferdinand Ernst. He grew up in Carinthia and received religious and scholarly training from Jesuits. After the deaths of his brothers Karl in 1603 and Johann Karl in 1619, he was designated his father's successor. He became Archduke of Austria in 1621, King of Hungary on 8 December 1625 and King of Bohemia on 27 November 1627. In 1631 he married his cousin Maria Anna of Spain.

After Albrecht von Wallenstein's assassination, Ferdinand took command of the imperial army on 2 May 1634. He regained Regensburg in July and Donauwörth in August, and in September won the decisive Battle of Nördlingen with Spanish forces under Cardinal Infante Ferdinand, although his personal part in it was limited. He was elected King of the Romans on 22 December 1636 and became emperor on his father's death on 15 February 1637, when much of the empire had been devastated by two decades of war. By 1640 he had permanently lost control of northern Germany.

Peace negotiations began in Münster and Osnabrück in 1644 and lasted until 1648 while fighting went on. He suffered defeat at Jankau on 6 March 1645, after which a Swedish army advanced to Vienna. In the Peace of Linz of 1645 he guaranteed the Hungarian estates freedom of religion for Protestants. Spanish support ceased in 1645, and his instructions to his chief negotiator, Maximilian von Trauttmansdorff, show that he was ready to surrender more than was in the end necessary.

The Peace of Westphalia cost the empire territory: the Three Bishoprics went to France, Sweden received Rügen and Western Pomerania, and the Netherlands and Switzerland gained full independence. The imperial estates won the right to form alliances with foreign powers, and Ferdinand's attempt at absolutist rule of the empire failed. In his own lands his power was greater than his predecessors' before 1618. He restructured the Aulic Council and summoned the last traditional Reichstag in 1652.

Ferdinand died on 2 April 1657 and rests in the Capuchin Crypt in Vienna. His son Leopold I succeeded him after the death of his elder son Ferdinand IV in 1654. He was a patron of music and the first Habsburg monarch recognised as a composer; some of his masses, motets and hymns survive in manuscript.
ferdinand-lassalle: Ferdinand Lassal, who later adopted the French spelling Lassalle, was born in Breslau, now Wrocław, on 11 April 1825. His Jewish family had moved to Prussian Silesia from Poland in the late 18th century, and his father, Heymann Lassal, a prosperous wholesale silk merchant, had trained for a rabbinical career. A diary he kept as a boy shows a quick-witted, ambitious youth, sensitive about his Jewishness and his provincial background. After passing his matriculation examination in 1843 he studied at the universities of Breslau and Berlin, where he discovered Hegel, whose philosophy he later described as a second birth.

In 1846 Lassalle met Countess Sophie von Hatzfeldt, unhappily married to Count Edmund von Hatzfeldt-Kinsweiler, and spent the next eight years almost entirely on her legal claims against her husband. The case brought him public renown and, in 1848, a sentence of two months for criminal libel; arrested for complicity in the theft of documents, he was acquitted at Cologne in August 1848. There he met Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. Engels disliked his ostentation, while Marx was more tolerant, though a report of 1855 left him mistrustful. Lassalle also wrote Heraclitus the Obscure (1857) and The System of Acquired Rights (1861).

In April 1862 he gave two lectures in Berlin arguing that a constitution is the factual power relationship in a society written down, and that the working class should form its own party. In 1863 he founded the General German Workers' Association, whose platform called for socialism through state-aided producers' co-operatives won by universal suffrage. He negotiated secretly with Otto von Bismarck, hoping to ally the workers' movement with the conservative state against the liberal bourgeoisie.

In the summer of 1864 Lassalle became engaged to Helene von Dönniges, daughter of a Bavarian diplomat. Her family opposed the match because of his Jewish origins and political notoriety, and she was pressured into renouncing him for a previous suitor, Yanko von Rakowitza. Lassalle challenged her father to a duel; he declined, and Rakowitza accepted in his place. Lassalle was killed in a duel on 31 August 1864, aged 39.

The association then had only a few thousand members, but under Johann Baptist von Schweitzer it kept Lassalle's centralised organisation and pro-governmental tactics. In 1875 it merged with the Social Democratic Workers' Party at the Gotha Congress to form what became the Social Democratic Party of Germany, whose programme drew on his demand for state-aided co-operatives. Marx thought his state socialism a misunderstanding of his own theories.
ferdinand-magellan: Magellan was born in northern Portugal, possibly around 1480. His father, Pedro de Magalhães, was a minor member of the Portuguese nobility and mayor of the town, and his mother was Alda de Mezquita. He was brought up as a page of Queen Eleanor, consort of King John II, and in 1495 he entered the service of Manuel I.

In March 1505 he enlisted in the fleet sent to host Francisco de Almeida as the first viceroy of Portuguese India, and he remained there eight years. He took part in the battle of Cannanore in 1506, where he was wounded, and the Battle of Diu in 1509. In 1511, under Afonso de Albuquerque, he and his friend Francisco Serrão took part in the conquest of Malacca. Serrão went on to the Moluccas, and his letters to Magellan later gave decisive information about the spice-producing territories.

King Manuel I repeatedly rejected Magellan's proposals for expeditions to the Spice Islands. Magellan then offered the project to Charles I of Spain, who approved it. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 Portugal was to control the eastern routes around the Cape of Good Hope, so Magellan proposed a southwestern passage around South America. He was given command of the five-ship Armada of Molucca and sailed in August 1519 with about 270 men. King Manuel did all he could to disrupt the preparations, and a Portuguese fleet sent after him failed to capture him.

The fleet crossed the Atlantic and went south to Patagonia. Despite storms and mutinies, it passed through the Strait of Magellan into the sea Magellan renamed the Mar Pacifico, landed at Guam and reached the Philippines. Magellan converted as many as 2,200 locals to Christianity, including Rajah Humabon of Cebu, but Lapulapu, the leader of Mactan, resisted. On the morning of 27 April 1521 Magellan sailed to Mactan with a small force and was killed in the battle that followed.

Antonio Pigafetta and Ginés de Mafra left accounts of the death. Lapulapu refused a ransom of copper and iron for the body. Under Juan Sebastián Elcano the expedition reached the Spice Islands, and the ship Elcano commanded returned to Spain in September 1522, completing the first circumnavigation of Earth. In the aftermath Magellan was widely discredited in Spain and Portugal. Some in Portugal regarded him as a traitor for having sailed for Spain.
ferdinand-marcos: Ferdinand Marcos was born in Sarrat, Ilocos Norte, on 11 September 1917. His father, Mariano Marcos, was a lawyer who represented Ilocos Norte in the House of Representatives from 1925 to 1931. Marcos studied law at the University of the Philippines, where he was a national rifle champion. In 1935 Julio Nalundasan, who had defeated Mariano Marcos in two elections, was shot dead at his home. Ferdinand and his uncle were convicted of the murder, but the conviction was overturned on appeal. He fought the Japanese after joining the United States Army in 1941. Researchers later found that most stories about his military service were inaccurate or untrue.

Marcos won his father's former seat in 1949, sat in the House of Representatives until 1959, in the Senate from 1959 to 1965, and was Senate president from 1963 to 1965. He was elected president in 1965 and re-elected in 1969. His early policies centred on massive infrastructure construction, funded by foreign lending. A balance of payments crisis in 1969 and growing Philippine involvement in the Vietnam War then triggered social unrest.
